title: Dysfunctional information sharing on WhatsApp and Facebook: The role of political talk, cross-cutting exposure and social corrections
screen_reason: Nationally representative survey of 1,615 Brazilian internet users (21 May - 3 July 2019) reporting the share of respondents who recall having shared a news story that turned out to be exaggerated or made up in the past month, separately for Facebook (25.94%) and WhatsApp (28.67%), and the share who recall sharing a story they already thought was made up or exaggerated (Facebook 13.19%, WhatsApp 14.36%). These are self-reported sharing of misinformation with an explicit denominator = RECALL (sharing).

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who recall sharing on Facebook in the past month a news story that seemed accurate at the time but was later found to be exaggerated or made up
estimates.denominator: Brazilian internet users who use WhatsApp, N=1,615 (quota sample: 1,431 online panel + 184 random digit dial); Facebook items were asked only of the 89% who use Facebook, whose exact n is not reported
estimates.definition: Answered 'yes' to: 'In the past month, do you recall sharing a news story that seemed accurate at the time, but you later found out was exaggerated or made up on Facebook?'
estimates.misinfo_def: "we use the term misinformation to apply broadly to the phenomenon of sharing (intentionally or accidentally), being exposed to, or believing in verifiably false information"
estimates.n: 1,615 respondents (Facebook items restricted to the 89% who use Facebook)
estimates.source_quote: Table 1. Frequency of dysfunctional sharing. Type of Sharing Frequency Accidental Sharing on Facebook Yes 25.94 % No 55.05 % Don’t know/Don’t remember 19.01 %
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent recall over a one-month window; the authors state the measure reflects what respondents perceive to be misinformation, not verified content, and can only capture sharing the respondent became aware of.
estimates.moderator_quote: We conducted a survey with a nationally representative sample of Internet users in Brazil (N = 1615), using demographic quotas to proportionally represent regional differences based on age, gender, and education.
estimates.notes: The 25.94% is the table value; the Results text rounds it to 25%. The denominator includes the 19.01% who said they did not remember, so this is a share of all Facebook-using respondents, not a valid percentage. Topic coded general_news because the item says 'a news story' with no political restriction, even though the paper frames the study around political misinformation.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons. (1) Social-correction items in Table 4: experiencing a correction (Facebook 26.44%, WhatsApp 36.05%), witnessing one (41.96% / 46.78%) and performing one (32.03% / 40.15%). Experiencing a correction ('I was told the news I had shared was exaggerated, inaccurate, or made up') arguably implies the respondent shared misinformation and could be read as a third RECALL sharing measure with a different informant; witnessing ('I saw someone else being called out') is closer to a recall of others' misinformation sharing. I left all three out because the construct being measured is corrective behaviour in the respondent's network, not the respondent's own exposure to or sharing of misinformation, and because the reported percentages are valid percentages on a shifting base (the N column in Table 4 does not correspond to the denominator of the percentage: 427 is 26.4% of 1,615, but 597 is not 36.05% of 1,615). An adjudicator who counts 'was told what I shared was false' as sharing recall should add those two rows. (2) 'Sharing to correct' ('I shared news that I knew was inaccurate to alert others that it was circulating') is used as a regression control but no frequency is reported for it. (3) Political talk, cross-cutting exposure, WhatsApp group membership, political extremism, misinformed-belief and political-knowledge distributions are not misinformation exposure or sharing. (4) The misinformed-beliefs battery (15 statements, 10 false) measures belief, which the instructions exclude, and no share of respondents endorsing falsehoods is reported anyway. (5) 'roughly half of all images circulating through the service were likely altered or distorted to convey false information' is cited from Tardaguila et al. via First Draft, not this study's data, so R8 forbids keeping it. (6) The exact n for the Facebook items is not given; only '89% of the sample' is stated, so I did not compute it. NOTE ON QUOTES: the text file keeps the PDF's end-of-line hyphenation, so some quotes contain a broken word ("acknowl- edged", "exagger- ated", "(intention- ally"); that is the text file's rendering of the sentence, not a transcription error, and the quotes are otherwise exact contiguous spans.

rob.design: Cross-sectional survey of a nationally representative quota sample of Brazilian internet users, N=1,615, restricted to WhatsApp users; fielded by Ibope 21 May - 3 July 2019, combining an online nonprobability panel (n=1,431, completion rate 25%) with random digit dial interviews (n=184, AAPOR RR1 = 26%) added to reach lower-education and older respondents; quotas on region, age, gender and education; sample size set for a 2% margin of error. All misinformation measures are single-item self-reports with a one-month recall window and a yes/no/don't-remember response set. The authors state the limitations plainly: the measures reflect perceived rather than verified misinformation, capture only sharing the respondent became aware of, and may be affected by desirability bias; the design is cross-sectional so no causal claims.
rob.item6_quote: For the purposes of this study, we use the term misinformation to apply broadly to the phenomenon of sharing (intention- ally or accidentally), being exposed to, or believing in verifiably false information.
